summary: Points out that the FTP mail protocol of the day had no way to state the author, title and date of a message, so each system sent them in its own format and programs struggled to process mail. The authors propose standardizing header information.

eli5.summary: Letters had no agreed place to write who sent them and when, so each computer did it differently. This note suggests everyone write it the same way.

questions: what headers did early arpanet mail use
subtitle: An interim proposal to give network mail a standard From, Date and Subject header.

tldr.problem: The FTP mail protocol had no way to specify author, title and date, so each system sent them in its own format and programs could not process incoming mail.
tldr.mechanism: The authors propose a simple header block of FROM, DATE and SUBJECT lines, plus optional keyword lines, followed by a blank line and the message.
tldr.outcome: It is offered as a quick interim fix; the long-term answer is thought to be new mail protocol commands, and RFC 680 later updated it.

facts.label: Required header items
facts.value: FROM, DATE, SUBJECT (each at most once)

today: RFC 561 has no formal status recorded and was updated by RFC 680. It was an interim proposal pending changes to the mail protocol itself.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
The current FTP mail protocol makes no provision for explicitly specifying header information such as author, title and date. Many systems send that information, but each in a different format. As a result it is next to impossible for a system or user program to intelligently process incoming mail.

The long-term solution is probably to add commands for this information to the mail protocol command space, as suggested in RFC 524. This RFC proposes a more quickly implemented interim solution.
sections.eli5: Everyone wrote the sender and date differently, so computers could not read them. The fix is one shared way to write them.

sections.title: The Proposed Header Syntax
sections.content:
The text of network mail, whether sent over the FTP Telnet connection with the MAIL command or over a separate data connection with MLFL, would be a header, then a blank line, then the message. The header has a FROM: item (user AT host), a DATE: item (date, four-digit time and zone) and a SUBJECT: item, plus any number of other keyword: lines.

The example in the RFC begins with From: White at SRI-ARC, a date of 24 JUL 1973 1527-PDT, a subject and a NIC number.
sections.eli5: The first lines of every letter say who it is from, the date, and what it is about. Then there is a blank line and the letter itself.

sections.title: Rules and Recommendations
sections.content:
The From, Date and Subject items may each appear at most once, in any order, but they must come before all other keyword items. The case of keywords is insignificant, so From, from and FROM are equivalent. The format of the user name is not legislated, except that spaces are excluded, and no provision is made for multiple authors.

The authors recommend that mail-sending subsystems that prefix header information be modified accordingly, and that other hosts recommend these conventions to their users.
sections.eli5: The main lines can come in any order, capital letters do not matter, and each letter has one author.

data.title: Example mail text
data.code:
From: White at SRI-ARC
Date: 24 JUL 1973 1527-PDT
Subject: Multi-Site Journal Meeting Announcement
NIC: 17996

At 10 AM Wednesday 25-JULY there will be a meeting
to discuss a Multi-Site Journal in the context of
the Utility.  Y'all be here.
